Practice-relevant•Peer-reviewed randomized clinical trial•October 13, 2026

Low-intensity resource referral misses its caregiver self-efficacy endpoint

In a single-blind randomized trial, CommunityRx-Dementia did not improve 12-month caregiver self-efficacy or most prespecified outcomes among 133 caregivers with health-related social risks, although emergency-department use was lower (IRR 0.41, 95% CI 0.19-0.90).

Key quantitative results: Among caregivers with health-related social risks, 12-month self-efficacy was 3.5 in both groups (OR 0.80, 95% CI 0.30-2.09), so the primary endpoint was not met.

Clinical TrialsManagementCaregiver support

Added October 14, 2026 · DOI:10.1111/jgs.70684; PMID:42869650; NCT04146545

Evidence summaryDesign, results, and what changed

Thirty-second field brief

A personalized community-resource list, text-based navigation and online finder did not improve the trial's primary caregiver self-efficacy outcome in the prespecified higher-need group. Lower emergency-department use is clinically interesting but was one of several secondary outcomes and needs replication. The result argues against assuming that high engagement with a low-intensity referral service translates into broad caregiver benefit.

Study design

English-speaking dementia caregivers living in 62 ZIP codes around one urban academic medical center were randomized to usual care or usual care plus CommunityRx-Dementia. The intervention supplied education about common needs, a personalized list of nearby resources, text access to a navigator and an online resource finder. The prespecified primary analysis included 133 caregivers with at least one baseline health-related social risk; a post hoc analysis included 210 caregivers without such risks. Outcomes were assessed at 12 months.

Key quantitative results

  • Among caregivers with health-related social risks, 12-month self-efficacy was 3.5 in both groups (OR 0.80, 95% CI 0.30-2.09), so the primary endpoint was not met.
  • Loneliness was 41% versus 50% (OR 0.62, 95% CI 0.24-1.59), needing help 23% versus 34% (OR 0.80, 95% CI 0.30-2.11) and hospitalizations 0.1 versus 0.2 (IRR 0.42, 95% CI 0.14-1.30); none differed significantly.
  • Emergency-department utilization was lower with the intervention, 0.3 versus 0.7 visits (IRR 0.41, 95% CI 0.19-0.90). In the post hoc subgroup without baseline social risks, most outcomes were similar, while odds of needing help were lower (OR 0.31, 95% CI 0.12-0.83).
  • Engagement was high: 94% of caregivers with social risks texted a navigator and 31% requested additional resource information.

What changed

A completed randomized trial now provides controlled evidence that a scalable, low-intensity community-resource referral can achieve high engagement but does not by itself improve broad caregiver self-efficacy; its emergency-use signal remains secondary and exploratory for implementation decisions.

Strength of evidence

Moderate randomized evidence for the null primary outcome, with prespecified analysis and 12-month follow-up. Confidence in the emergency-department finding is lower because it was one of several secondary outcomes, event counts were self-reported, confidence intervals for other utilization outcomes were wide and the study was limited to one urban region.

Clinical and field impactInterpretation, implementation, and access

Clinical significance

Health systems should not present resource referral alone as a proven way to improve caregiver self-efficacy. The lower emergency-use signal may justify a larger implementation trial with verified utilization and prespecified multiplicity control, especially among caregivers facing social risks.

Field medical relevance

Directly relevant to caregiver-support program design, social-care navigation, health-equity implementation and discussions about which outcomes a low-touch intervention can reasonably change.

Access or reimbursement relevance

The intervention was designed to connect caregivers with local resources, but the study did not establish service availability outside the trial geography, reimbursement, scalable navigator capacity or coverage. Any reduction in access barriers remains unproven as a system-level outcome.

Likely questionsWhat you may hear and what the evidence supports
Did CommunityRx-Dementia meet its primary endpoint?
No. Twelve-month caregiver self-efficacy was 3.5 in both groups, with OR 0.80 (95% CI 0.30-2.09).
Does the emergency-department result establish reduced acute-care use?
Not yet. It was a favorable secondary result based on self-report and should be confirmed in a larger trial using adjudicated utilization data.
Does the trial support reimbursement or a formal care standard?
No. It supplies intervention evidence but no guideline endorsement, payment decision or standardized implementation requirement.
Critique and limitationsBias, uncertainty, and missing evidence
  • Single urban academic-center geography and English-speaking text-message users
  • Primary analysis included only 133 caregivers with baseline social risks
  • Emergency visits and hospitalizations were self-reported
  • Multiple secondary outcomes and a post hoc lower-risk subgroup
  • The primary endpoint and most prespecified secondary outcomes were null
  • No evidence of long-term sustainability, cost-effectiveness or reimbursement
